Write tests that actually fail when the behavior they claim to cover breaks. A recurring failure mode across these discussions is assertions and fixtures that pass regardless of whether the implementation is correct: `deepEqual` on a chain that short-circuits on `undefined`, a loose upper bound (`toBeLessThan(naive / 10)`) that tolerates a wrong-but-plausible implementation, test fixtures that happen to satisfy the check trivially (e.g. every "overloaded" fixture also containing the word "overloaded" in its message, so the error-code branch is never independently exercised), or a helper that strips away exactly the variation it should be guarding (stripping all CLDR plural suffixes before comparing catalogs). Mocking a dependency at the wrong boundary has the same effect — stubbing out the real adapter instead of stubbing only `fetch` means the integration code path is never actually run.

To avoid this:
- Prefer exact-value or exact-invariant assertions over loose bounds when the behavior has a precise contract. If a per-image token cost should be flat regardless of payload size, assert equality of two different-sized inputs rather than "less than some big number."
- Make sure fixtures isolate the dimension under test: when testing an error-code check, use a neutral message; when testing a message check, use an unrecognized code. Don't let one fixture silently cover both.
- Prove a test actually catches a regression: mentally (or literally) break the implementation and confirm the new test fails. If removing the fix doesn't fail the test, the test isn't testing it.
- Mock only at the real system boundary (e.g. `fetch`, a subprocess) and drive the real adapter/SDK code through it, instead of mocking the component whose behavior you need to verify.
- Keep test fixtures honest: a fake server or fixture used to simulate failure/timeout/cancellation should not independently resolve the scenario (e.g. exiting on its own) in a way that lets the test pass without the production code doing its job — assert on the mechanism (e.g. `signal=SIGTERM`), not just the outcome.
